EntertainmentTab.title: ‘They pulled a guy’s face off. It’s my favourite bit!’ Linda Cardellini on Freaks and Geeks, Mad Men and slasher horror Crystal Lake
EntertainmentTab.text:
‘The first time I had the tooth in my hand,” says Linda Cardellini, “I thought, ‘Oh my God, this is what I’m doing.’” The star of Freaks and Geeks, ER, Dead to Me, Mad Men and DTF St Louis (for which she recently won an Emmy) is talking about her pivot towards full-blown horror. In Crystal Lake, the prequel to the Friday the 13th movies, Cardellini plays Pamela Voorhees, the original slasher of the 1980 film. The tooth, by the way, is human and gets embedded in Pam’s knuckle – until she yanks it out with a gruesome, revolting slurping sound.

Casual filmgoers may associate Friday the 13th with Jason, the hockey-mask-wearing serial killer. But aficionados will know that Pam, Jason’s mother, is the villain of the first movie. “He didn’t even have the mask until the third movie,” says Cardellini, who has clearly done her homework. “Pam is the original killer, in vengeance of his death.” (There is some massaging of previous storylines in Crystal Lake, such as moving Jason’s drowning from the 1950s to the early 70s, but since the franchise is flexible enough to have sent Jason into space at one point, a bit of timeline tweaking feels fair game.)

The Friday the 13th franchise has a devoted audience – and Crystal Lake’s showrunner, Brad Caleb Kane, is among them. “He’s such a fan,” says Cardellini. “I felt he would have an idea of what fans were wanting.” Kane wrote the part specifically for her, after seeing her in Netflix thriller Dead to Me, which came as a surprise. “My biggest question was, ‘How did I become the person at the front of your mind for this?’” she laughs. Did they feel any pressure in taking Friday the 13th on? “It’s daunting, but hopefully it’s an opportunity to see more of something that didn’t really get its own avenue.”

Anyone who grew up in the 1980s and 90s, as Cardellini did (she is 51), will remember sleepovers with rented VHS tapes and a lot of screaming whenever Freddy Krueger, Michael Myers or Jason Voorhees appeared on screen. “It was forbidden fruit, almost,” she says. “You weren’t supposed to be able to watch it, but you would. And not only the gore but the sexuality – all the things you’re not supposed to be watching. I think it is part of the allure when you’re young. It seems off-limits and rebellious.”

She liked the jump scares and the gore, which is handy, because Crystal Lake is full of them. One vivid sequence involves an astronomical amount of blood. “We reserved a whole week for that,” she says, which is highly unusual for TV, as it tends to move quickly. It had to be precisely planned and choreographed, not least because Cardellini’s hair in the show is lighter, and they soon found that the fake blood stained it pink.

“Even the guy’s face coming off is done on the day with prosthetics, instead of CGI. It’s what you’re actually looking at, which helps with your reaction.” So that wasn’t done in post-production? “No! They pulled it off with fishing wire. So I saw it for the first time as it came off. It stuck with me for a while, because it’s disgusting.” It proved to be one of her highlights. “That’s actually one of my favourite parts of the show. It’s like a blood opera.”

Crystal Lake arrives on a new wave of mainstream horror, from films such as Obsession and Backrooms to Carrie and Widow’s Bay on TV. Why does Cardellini think horror is having a moment? “It’s a great question. I can imagine there’s something about the experience of it that is very present – and it’s a controlled fear, because you know that in a few hours, you will have a resolution. Maybe that is digestible.”

Recently, Cardellini was backstage at a screening of the show at New York Comic Con. “There was some gasping and yelling and cheers – and afterwards, a laugh. That’s when you’re like, ‘OK, this is great, because that’s what the movies did.’ They made you afraid, then you laughed out loud. That is what we were going for. That felt good.”

Cardellini grew up in California and started acting in the mid-1990s. Her breakout was Freaks and Geeks, the Paul Feig/Judd Apatow teen comedy in which she played good girl gone bad Lindsay Weir. The early 80s-set series, a fond, witty look at teenage rebellion, burned bright and fast and was promptly cancelled by NBC in 2000, before its first season had finished airing. As well as Cardellini, it rocket-launched the careers of Seth Rogen, Jason Segel and Busy Philipps.

“If you got cancelled, you were just gone,” she says now. “You didn’t even know where it went. The idea that it would live on, once we weren’t going to make any more, just didn’t seem possible.” Through DVDs and word of mouth, though, Freaks and Geeks slowly became a classic of the high school TV genre. “That it had a life afterwards was a shock – and that it still has a life is amazing.”

On the subject of all-time-greatest TV series, Cardellini joined Mad Men in its sixth season, playing Sylvia Rosen, who has an affair with Don Draper. There was such secrecy around this that when she auditioned, names and details were changed. “I had no idea what I would be doing and [creator] Matt Weiner said, ‘Just trust me, it’s gonna get great.’ I think it was the first two scripts I got – I had one line. I thought, ‘What am I doing? What is this?’” But Weiner had told her it would be a great part and he was not lying. Not only does her character go on to remind Don of a sex worker from his youth, she also gets to leave him, triggering an obsession. “It unfolded like a surprise for me,” she says.

In September, Cardellini won her first Emmy for her role as Carol Love-Smernitch in HBO’s DTF St Louis. “I’ve been nominated before, but winning is a very different feeling,” she says. “It was a wonderful moment.” DTF St Louis is a singular series: Carol is married to American Sign Language interpreter Floyd, but is having an affair with his best friend Clark, a TV weatherman who rides a weird bike and likes to pretend to be a robot during sex. When Cardellini first heard about the show, she thought she knew how the story would go. “A love triangle between a married couple and a best friend, and somebody turns up dead,” she recalls. “But when I read it, I thought, ‘I’ve never read anything like this.’ Every time I thought I knew where it was going, it went somewhere else, in this beautiful, nuanced, very human way.”

The show is a strange, sweet meditation on loneliness, with an offbeat streak. Carol, for instance, is a part-time baseball umpire. “Since I’ve played an umpire, I’ve met so many people who have told me they are also umpires, and it’s people you don’t expect. Also, the parent attacks that they have to weather are pretty funny.” Could she still umpire a game? “Maybe Little League. I don’t know if I can handle the parents!”

That Emmy award now lives on the mantel of her fireplace. Her first appearance on TV was in 1994, when she was a contestant on the quizshow The Price Is Right. You can see it on YouTube – she won a fireplace. Hang on, it’s not the same fireplace is it? “I wish! I don’t have that fireplace any more because, oddly enough, I lost it in a fire.” You lost a fireplace in a fire? “I was working and put a lot of stuff in storage. The storage facility caught fire.” But she had kept it for a long time? “Oh, for years and years and years.”

Earlier this year, Cardellini filmed They Know, a psychological horror movie written and directed by Bill Hader, who also stars. “It’s definitely his incredibly extraordinary point of view,” she says, reluctant to give too much away beyond the fact she plays his ex-wife. The fact that it’s another horror does not mean, however, that Cardellini is in her scream queen era. “I like to change it up,” she says. “I went from DTF to Crystal Lake with one week in between. That seemed like a big left turn. So we’ll see what comes up.” She pauses and adds: “But you never know.”

GeneralTab.title: Curfew imposed in parts of central Paris and other cities after rioting across France
GeneralTab.text:
French authorities have imposed overnight curfews in parts of central Paris and other cities after a weekend of riots and looting across the country.

Police in Paris said a curfew would be in force between 23:00 local time (21:00 GMT) and 06:00 in Place de la République, where protesters had gathered over the weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area.

A ban on unauthorised gatherings has also been imposed in several other parts of the city centre.

Partial curfews variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings were announced for cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south as well as Lille and other towns in the north.

Earlier Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, who has been strongly criticised by opposition politicians over the preparedness for the disorder but whose resignation was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron, admitted police had "lost control" in some cities.

The protests began last month with students demanding better school conditions, but they have since escalated to take in a broader range of concerns, with numbers at demonstrations this weekend bolstered by trade unions and various protest groups.

More than 2,500 people have been arrested, officials said. One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency. About 1,000 police officers were injured.

Following a crisis meeting on Monday, the prime minister said local mayors were being given the power to implement curfews "where they need", without specifying which cities where they would be enforced.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, who did not rule out imposing a state of emergency in the country, said the government would also set aside money to help affected areas recover from the damage, and the funding would be recovered from those behind the violence.

"There will be a law that will be put in place to find ways of making sure that those who have damaged properties will have to pay," Lecornu said.

He also announced a partial unemployment fund for those who could not work as a result of the riots and looting.

GeneralTab.title: Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC
GeneralTab.text:
Ukrainians have died because Kyiv is still not receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks, according to a key adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov told the BBC that lives had been lost because there had not been time to warn citizens about ballistic missile strikes, saying: "It's dangerous... I think it's really very bad... People [have] already died."

The adviser also said restrictions to Ukraine's use of the Starlink internet network were ongoing.

The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine.

Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing last week, as a row with the Trump administrations over its controversial deal to import Russian oil sent relations to new lows.

Despite the denials from Washington, many in Kyiv suspect the issues are not a coincidence.

On Monday morning, Zelensky wrote on social media: "Overnight two ballistic missile attacks were reported on the capital, one without warning, the second with only minimal time to take shelter."

Hours earlier, an interview the president did with NBC was published, in which he said intelligence sharing had been restored after a three-day pause.

"We are very thankful for this," he said. "Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles."

But Beskrestnov told the BBC that American intelligence continued to be incomplete and inconsistent, and that the US had failed to provide a clear explanation for the issue.

"This looks very strange," he said. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not."

He continued: "And for example, last night we received it, but... one minute before the attack."

However, he said other collaboration with US continues, adding: "Intelligence data keeps flowing, and the issue is solely with the air raid alert component."

Beskrestnov also said the US had given no clarity about who was responsible for the ongoing restrictions to the Starlink internet network and its military service Starshield, which Kyiv uses to provide connectivity for drones, helicopters and military communications.

Last week, Starshield restricted the speed at which mobile units could move while staying connected to the network to 100mph (160km/h).

This has limited Ukraine's ability to shoot down incoming drones or to launch mid-range drone attacks into Russian-occupied areas.

Starlink owner Elon Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, which was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions. Trump has denied involvement.

Beskrestnov said he thought both issues occurring at the same time was "probably" a deliberate move to put pressure on Ukraine.

He told BBC News: "It's probably the United States trying to say [to] us, 'let's have the conversation, negotiation with Russia, you should find the compromise'."

Beskrestnov also said Ukraine had its own radar data to provide some limited warning of incoming attacks, but was urgently looking into using alternative communication systems.

He added: "Now we understand that something begins to happen with Starlink, and we're not sure what will be the next step.

"We understand that we should be prepared for some problems in future. And now we're thinking about an alternative for Starlink, not only for air defence, for communication between our forces, between our staff, for civilians also, because we don't know what we should expect in future regarding Starlink."

On Monday, when asked about intelligence sharing, Trump said: "We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given us nothing."

GeneralTab.title: Chancellor rejects calls to raise Capital Gains Tax in Budget
GeneralTab.text:
Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey has dismissed calls from some Labour MPs to increase Capital Gains Tax (CGT) when he hands down his first Budget.

Cabinet ministers Wes Streeting and Louise Haigh both previously voiced support for raising CGT before Andy Burnham became prime minister in July.

Ahead of next week's Budget, Healey ruled out lifting CGT - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value, such as shares in a company or properties which are not primary residences.

The move followed warnings that it could end up costing the government money if wealthy people leave the country or defer selling off assets, the Times newspaper reported.

The chancellor has previously indicated he wanted the UK to be a country of wealth creation, saying government policies should lift confidence, investment and profit.

Burnham has faced warnings against lifting CGT. His former adviser and Goldman Sachs Chief Economist Lord Jim O'Neill suggested it would send "the wrong message to business".

But, influential Labour figures had pushed for equalising CGT and income tax, with the former generally attracting a lower tax rate.

Louise Haigh, a key ally of the prime minister, had suggested capital gains should go up to be closer to income tax, before she became Burnham's first secretary of state.

Defence secretary Wes Streeting called for a "wealth tax that works" in May, shortly after resigning as a minister in former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's government.

Healey already ruled out levelling the two tax rates, according to the Financial Times, external.

In a pre-Budget speech on Tuesday, Tory leader Kemi Badenoch is expected to urge the government to drop its spending plans and reduce its borrowing.

GeneralTab.title: Vinted blocks French looters listing stolen goods for sale
GeneralTab.text:
Vinted says it has removed listings of items believed to have been looted from shops during the ongoing riots in France.

The second hand re-selling platform said following the weekend's disorder it had "taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to looting".

Shops across several French cities were broken into and ransacked during the outbreak of riots over the weekend.

"The sale of stolen goods, or soliciting them, is strictly prohibited on Vinted, and we have zero tolerance for it," a spokesperson for the company said.

Widespread looting was reported across Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas after protests against the cost of living and public spending turned into riots, leading to the arrests of at least 1,200 people.

More than 2,000 businesses were directly impacted by the weekend's violence, according to the head of the Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI).

Alain Di Crescenzo told France's broadcaster RTL that the riots led to hundreds of millions of euros worth of damage.

Groups of rioters, some wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings as well as looting businesses.

Those that stole goods now appear to be looking to sell them on fast.

"Since this weekend, our teams have taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to the looting, and we have stepped up monitoring of suspicious listings," Vinted told the BBC.

"When our rules are breached, we act against the accounts involved, up to permanent bans."

The company said it was working with French authorities and the police, and was adapting its "processes to detect and counter emerging risks and malicious behaviour".

eBay has not noted any increase in listings linked to the looting in France, but said it works with law enforcement to investigate suspected stolen goods and takes appropriate action, including removing listings and taking action against sellers, when authorities confirm an item is stolen.

GeneralTab.title: Home sellers cut asking prices on 3,000 properties a day, says Rightmove
GeneralTab.text:
Home sellers cut asking prices on more than 3,000 properties a day on average in Britain during September, according to figures from Rightmove shared exclusively with the BBC.

The property website said the total was the highest of any month for 15 years and was driven, in part, by a glut of homes on the market and some sellers setting unrealistic expectations.

The proportion of listed homes that eventually had a price cut peaked in 2023 and has remained relatively high since.

One seller - Stewart, from Leicester - said some properties were being filtered out of buyers' search results.

He sold one property, and was now selling his late mother's, and both included an element of leasehold which more buyers have been avoiding. However, he said no one thing defined whether a property would sell at a certain price.

"Part of the issue is trying to work out the right selling price. Properties were on the market high and low but were not selling," he said.

He turned down an offer made on his home a day after it was listed. It was below the asking price and he held out for better offers that never came. In the end, he sold after 18 months for £30,000 less than the original asking price.

Colleen Babcock, of Rightmove, said: "Once a home has been on the market for a while and then has a price reduction, some buyers start asking questions, even when there is nothing wrong with the property.

"In a market with so much choice, first impressions matter."

Property portals say buyers are now having to be choosy, with many working to a tight budget as mortgage rates have risen to three-year highs.

articles.text:
Ukrainians have died because Kyiv is still not receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks, according to a key adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov told the BBC that lives had been lost because there had not been time to warn citizens about ballistic missile strikes, saying: "It's dangerous... I think it's really very bad... People [have] already died."

The adviser also said restrictions to Ukraine's use of the Starlink internet network were ongoing.

The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine.

Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing last week, as a row with the Trump administrations over its controversial deal to import Russian oil sent relations to new lows.

Despite the denials from Washington, many in Kyiv suspect the issues are not a coincidence.

On Monday morning, Zelensky wrote on social media: "Overnight two ballistic missile attacks were reported on the capital, one without warning, the second with only minimal time to take shelter."

Hours earlier, an interview the president did with NBC was published, in which he said intelligence sharing had been restored after a three-day pause.

"We are very thankful for this," he said. "Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles."

But Beskrestnov told the BBC that American intelligence continued to be incomplete and inconsistent, and that the US had failed to provide a clear explanation for the issue.

"This looks very strange," he said. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not."

He continued: "And for example, last night we received it, but... one minute before the attack."

However, he said other collaboration with US continues, adding: "Intelligence data keeps flowing, and the issue is solely with the air raid alert component."

Beskrestnov also said the US had given no clarity about who was responsible for the ongoing restrictions to the Starlink internet network and its military service Starshield, which Kyiv uses to provide connectivity for drones, helicopters and military communications.

Last week, Starshield restricted the speed at which mobile units could move while staying connected to the network to 100mph (160km/h).

This has limited Ukraine's ability to shoot down incoming drones or to launch mid-range drone attacks into Russian-occupied areas.

Starlink owner Elon Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, which was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions. Trump has denied involvement.

Beskrestnov said he thought both issues occurring at the same time was "probably" a deliberate move to put pressure on Ukraine.

He told BBC News: "It's probably the United States trying to say [to] us, 'let's have the conversation, negotiation with Russia, you should find the compromise'."

Beskrestnov also said Ukraine had its own radar data to provide some limited warning of incoming attacks, but was urgently looking into using alternative communication systems.

He added: "Now we understand that something begins to happen with Starlink, and we're not sure what will be the next step.

"We understand that we should be prepared for some problems in future. And now we're thinking about an alternative for Starlink, not only for air defence, for communication between our forces, between our staff, for civilians also, because we don't know what we should expect in future regarding Starlink."

On Monday, when asked about intelligence sharing, Trump said: "We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given us nothing."

articles.title: Chancellor rejects calls to raise Capital Gains Tax in Budget
articles.text:
Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey has dismissed calls from some Labour MPs to increase Capital Gains Tax (CGT) when he hands down his first Budget.

Cabinet ministers Wes Streeting and Louise Haigh both previously voiced support for raising CGT before Andy Burnham became prime minister in July.

Ahead of next week's Budget, Healey ruled out lifting CGT - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value, such as shares in a company or properties which are not primary residences.

The move followed warnings that it could end up costing the government money if wealthy people leave the country or defer selling off assets, the Times newspaper reported.

The chancellor has previously indicated he wanted the UK to be a country of wealth creation, saying government policies should lift confidence, investment and profit.

Burnham has faced warnings against lifting CGT. His former adviser and Goldman Sachs Chief Economist Lord Jim O'Neill suggested it would send "the wrong message to business".

But, influential Labour figures had pushed for equalising CGT and income tax, with the former generally attracting a lower tax rate.

Louise Haigh, a key ally of the prime minister, had suggested capital gains should go up to be closer to income tax, before she became Burnham's first secretary of state.

Defence secretary Wes Streeting called for a "wealth tax that works" in May, shortly after resigning as a minister in former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's government.

Healey already ruled out levelling the two tax rates, according to the Financial Times, external.

In a pre-Budget speech on Tuesday, Tory leader Kemi Badenoch is expected to urge the government to drop its spending plans and reduce its borrowing.

articles.title: Burnham vows end to 'rip-off parking charges' under new rules
articles.text:
Drivers will be given the right to challenge "rip off" private parking charges and more grace when using private providers under new rules set out by Andy Burnham.

The Prime Minister announced the changes after drivers repeatedly raised concerns penalties issued by private providers were too harsh and left motorists unfairly penalised.

In one case, a woman was taken to court in a £1,906 claim after taking longer than five minutes to pay at a car park in Derby. The charge was eventually dropped.

Private car parks already have an industry code of practice, but the RAC motoring group said the government's changes would protect drivers from the "poor practices of some private parking companies".

Burnham, the prime minister, said: "Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your numberplate wrong shouldn't end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat.

"These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I'm putting a stop to them."

The new rules will give drivers:

Operators who do not comply risk losing access to DVLA data, making it far more difficult to pursue the car's owner even if they do issue a charge.

Private car parks are different to council-owned car parks and streets. RAC analysis of government data showed a record 17 million private parking tickets were issued in 2025/2026 - a 17% increase from a year earlier.

With each charge worth up to £100, the data, analysed by the Press Association and the RAC Foundation, suggests drivers could collectively face private parking charges worth more than £4.6m each day.

The yellow and black envelope of a Penalty Charge Notice, or PCN, is a dreaded sight for motorists returning to their car.

The AA has warned some drivers pay up even if they have done nothing wrong, just to avoid the hassle. It said people felt they would not get a fair hearing if they appealed fines, with many saying they feared legal action.

The current private parking industry Code of Practice, created by the British Parking Association and the International Parking Community, was introduced in 2024.

But the culture of motorists feeling they have been harshly penalised has spurred the government to present a formalised code to Parliament.

The British Parking Association told the BBC it welcomed the changes, but said "many of the principles within the new framework are already reflected in the existing voluntary Code of Practice".

The new Code will apply in England, Scotland and Wales after motorists said they wanted independent oversight of the private parking industry.

Jack Cousens, head of roads policy at the AA, said drivers "finally have something which could offer them better protections against the worst private parking operators". He said in the past they have "aggressively attacked drivers to the point where many simply pay up".

But the RAC's head of policy Simon Williams said it wasn't the leap his firm had been campaigning for. He called for the banning of debt recovery fees being added on top of PCNs and said the current industry-run appeals bodies should be replaced by a single independent one.

The government said it will be consulting on the issue of debt recovery fees, as well as other recommendation from the Competition and Markets Authority.

articles.title: Woman says she 'closed eyes and tried not to be there' during alleged Russell Brand rape
articles.text:
A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand at a bar told the police "I just closed my eyes and tried not to be there" while the attack was taking place.

In a 2023 video interview with an officer shown to the jury at his trial, the woman said she had been speaking to Brand about him hosting the Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth when he allegedly sexually assaulted her.

Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to all seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.

The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009.

The woman told the Southwark Crown Court jury the "lad culture" of the 2000s stopped her from reporting the TV star.

She has accused Brand of grabbing her breasts at the bar in Soho in London in 2004 before dragging her into a toilet and allegedly raping her.

The pair had been attending a birthday party when the alleged incidents happened.

She said she waited two decades to come forward to the police because the thought of doing so "terrified" her.

She said his celebrity status meant "it would be his word against mine".

"I would be ostracised in my work environment or friends."

The complainant worked for MTV at the time and said she was often surrounded by famous people.

From behind a blue screen in the witness box she said times had changed.

In those days - she said - "you weren't believed as a woman and it was a lad culture of 'you wearing this, so you were asking for it' and all that rubbish you were told back then".

The complainant recalled Brand's "big weird grin" which she compared to the face of a clown as he allegedly launched forward and grabbed hold of her.

Brand's barrister, Ian Winter KC, suggested during cross examination that Brand and the woman went to the toilet consensually for a "kiss and a cuddle", but they abandoned the attempt to have a sexual encounter because of the filthy state of the flooded toilet.

The woman, who became tearful while giving evidence, has rejected this version of events.

She said she felt "dazed" after the alleged attack.

Pressed on her claim of being dragged into the toilets against her will, the defendant's barrister suggested it would have been "perfectly easy" for her to have struggled or asked for help.

She said she did not agree because he had been holding her quite strongly, saying "part of me was saying just get it over with so you can get out of here".

She described feeling numb and ashamed afterwards.

She told the jury she had later confided in a friend, telling them Brand had "tried to do it" - but held back from saying he had "succeeded" in raping her.

The woman told the prosecution barrister that she didn't even know at the time that the alleged oral attack would be legally considered as rape.

Earlier on Monday, the jury was shown a 2023 video interview with an officer in which the woman said she had been speaking to Brand about him hosting the Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth when he allegedly sexually assaulted her.

In her recorded interview with police, the woman said "he literally just grabbed my boobs out of nowhere in the middle of the conversation, just in the middle of a conversation and I just remember this weird maniacal grin, looming in front of me as he just grabbed my boobs".

A short while later, she said he "dragged me in the toilets" where the floor was flooded, before "he unzipped himself" and allegedly orally raped her.

She said the alleged rape was "swift", and left her "in disbelief and shock".

"The toilets were behind where he stood. It was literally just grab and pull. He was holding me quite strongly on the arm and pulled me in that direction," she said.

"Part of me was saying just get it over with so you can get out of here".

"I just closed my eyes and tried not to be there. I just remember it felt like a force. I definitely said I don't want to do this," she added.

After the alleged rape, the woman, who was in her 20s at the time, said Brand "turned to me and said 'oh I guess we should swap numbers now', like it was just all normal, like he hadn't just forced me to do that."

Brand denies all the charges he faces.

He has said that any sexual contact if it happened, would have been consensual.

The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks.

articles.title: Criminals in hospital set to lose benefits under new rules
articles.text:
Killers and serious sex offenders detained in hospital are among the criminals who will no longer receive benefits under proposals called for by victims' families.

Regulations due to be laid in Parliament on Tuesday seek to end the "double provision" and prevent serious criminals receiving up to £800 a month in universal credit over several years while already having their bed and board funded through the NHS while receiving psychiatric treatment.

The government said closing the loophole would save an estimated tens of millions of pounds annually.

The parents of Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley Kumar, who were killed by Valdo Calocane in Nottingham in 2023, welcomed the announcement.

The new regulations are expected to come into force early next year, subject to parliamentary approval.

Students Barnaby and Grace, and caretaker Ian Coates, were stabbed to death on 13 June 2023 by Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020.

Calocane was convicted of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility, and detained at a high-security hospital.

Barnaby's mother, Emma Webber, said: "This is long overdue, and simply the right thing to do.

"It was a disgrace that Calocane and offenders like him have ever received taxpayers' money.

"A hospital bed does not erase the egregious crimes committed, nor the destruction they have caused.

"Closing this loophole finally delivers some basic accountability that victims deserve."

Dr Sanjoy Kumar, Grace's father, said: "Our campaign has always been about accountability and fairness.

"Offenders with treatment orders already cost the taxpayer an enormous amount.

"On release, every offender gets help with housing and benefits.

"On the principle of fairness alone, we do not see why taxpayers should fund benefits while they are incarcerated."

The mother of Kennedi Westcarr-Sabaroche who was killed by her partner Gogoa Lois Tape in Hackney, east London, in April 2024, also lobbied for benefits paid to offenders in psychiatric hospitals to stop.

Tape was given a hospital order detaining him indefinitely after he pleaded guilty to manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility.

Kennedi's mother Linda Westcarr said: "For many victims' families, the question of whether serious offenders should continue to receive benefits raises understandable concerns about fairness, accountability and the values we uphold as a society.

"In my view, this is not simply a question of policy, it is also a matter of moral responsibility and ensuring that the impact on victims and their families is properly recognised."

The government said the move followed engagement with victims' families and experts as part of its plan to "put fairness back of the heart of the welfare system".

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said: "We said we'd act to tackle this gross unfairness and we're delivering on that promise.

"For too long these violent criminals have had their living costs paid by the taxpayer twice over, while their victims and families paid the price.

"That ends today because victims and taxpayers deserve a system that is fair and supports only those who genuinely need it."

Shadow Work and Pensions Secretary Helen Whately said: "Killers and rapists should not pocket benefits from a hospital bed.

"Labour has taken all year to stop a loophole it promised to close. And tens of millions saved barely makes a dent in the benefits bill Labour has let spiral out of control.

"The Conservatives would make universal credit a conditional, time-limited benefit, so taxpayers' money goes only to those who genuinely need it."

The proposed regulations apply to individuals subject to a Section 37 order under the Mental Health Act 1983 and a Section 57A order under the Criminal Procedure (Scotland) Act 1995.

The offences covered include manslaughter, attempted murder, wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm, rape, assault by penetration and rape of a child under 13.

Murder is not included because a hospital order is not an available sentence for the offence.

The change in regulation is expected to affect about 2,500 offenders already in hospital and approximately 200 a year in future, the government said, with the full financial impacts of the move due to be published as part of the 2026 Budget on 28 October.

articles.title: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of planting device had Saudi support, says court filing
articles.text:
A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government, according to a court filing, external in California.

US prosecutors claimed Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked for the AI firm, was in "frequent communication... with a member of the Saudi royal family", and say a member of the country's military paid for a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for his wife and son after his arrest.

The 35-year-old engineer was on Monday deemed a flight risk and denied bail, pending trial.

The Saudi government did not immediately respond to BBC requests for comment.

Alfozan had worked at OpenAI for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant an audio recorder.

The AI company discovered the device, which was plugged into the back of a TV in a conference meeting room and covered up with toilet paper, on 30 September.

A camera was placed in the room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering and appearing to look behind the television where the audio recorder had been inserted.

He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI was terminated.

The court filing claimed the suspect's alleged conduct could pose "a danger to the national security of the United States", because executives from the tech firm met with government officials in the room during the days the device was believed to have been installed.

It said Alfozan's arrest came three days before he was scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way itinerary with his wife and son.

Following the arrest, the document claims the defendant's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her US visa was expiring" and so she and her son were "permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia", and her husband intended to do the same.

On 10 October, the day after Alfozan was arrested, his wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar. They travelled on a one-way business class ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official.

"Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through," the prosecutors argued.

US district judge Alex Tse on Monday denied Alfozan's attorneys request for his release on bail, saying "there is a risk of non-appearance that is significant".

The FBI investigation is ongoing.

Alfozan was scheduled to ‌appear ⁠in federal court in San Francisco later on Monday. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£188,000) fine.

articles.title: Five ways El Niño is affecting the weather around the world
articles.text:
El Niño has been strengthening for several months now and is already having a significant impact on global weather patterns.

Countries including Indonesia, India and the United States have been experiencing droughts, floods and heatwaves in line with projections about how extreme weather events will be supercharged by the phenomenon.

The World Meteorological Agency says the record-breaking El Niño will strengthen further and persist until at least 2027.

Here are five ways its impact is already being felt around the world.

Indonesia, which typically trends drier and hotter in El Niño years, is battling its worst wildfire season since 2015.

This year, since January, at least 895,657 hectares of land – nearly six times the size of Greater London – have been burned.

This is more than twice the area burned last year without the influence of El Niño.

The wildfires have led to school closures and an increase in hospital admissions across Indonesia.

Millions of people in Sumatra and Kalimantan have been exposed to toxic haze from the fires and around 175,000 people have suffered from respiratory illness.

More than 40,000 cases – which range from coughs to bronchitis and more serious conditions like pneumonia – involve toddlers.

In the eastern Pacific, where El Niño tends to strengthen hurricane activity, it has been a very active season so far.

There have been 22 named storms and 12 hurricanes, including 10 major hurricanes.

This is already above the number that would typically develop in the whole of an average season, with two months left to go until its end.

Here, El Niño provides the ingredients of higher ocean temperatures and weaker winds high in the atmosphere, making it easier for storms to gain strength.

Hurricane Polo is one such example of this.

The hurricane experienced rapid intensification, producing wind gusts of 180 mph (285 kmh), fueled by the very warm waters produced by El Niño.

Polo was also one of three hurricanes churning away in the same basin at the same time, along with Odalys and Nolo.

Moreover, it has happened twice now in the space of a month.

Earlier in September, the energy produced by exceptional ocean heat resulted in three simultaneous hurricanes in the central and eastern Pacific: Lowell, Karina and Marie.

Until this year, the last time there had been three Pacific hurricanes at the same time was 2015.

In contrast, the Atlantic Ocean has remained eerily quiet.

El Nino has a tendency to increase wind shear in the north Atlantic, a factor which tears apart storms and limits formation.

There has only been one hurricane - Isaias - which made landfall in the Florida Panhandle and Alabama.

This was the latest forming hurricane on record in the satellite era (1960s onward).

Before this year, the record was 11 September, set in 2002 and 2013.

In an average season, there would have been 10 named storms, five hurricanes and two major hurricanes by this point.

This year, however, there have only been eight tropical storms: Arthur, Bertha, Cristobal, Dolly, Edouard, Fay, Gonzalo and Hanna.

Further west in the Pacific, it's also been an active season in eastern China and Japan as storms including Maysak and Dujuan have brought recent widespread floods and landslides.

According to the Japanese Meteorological Agency, there have been 10 tropical cyclones forming in the western Pacific Ocean - the highest number in a season since 1966.

During El Niño the warmer Pacific brings changes to wind patterns, meaning cyclones tend to form further east, away from Japan and east China.

However, this means there is a bigger distance and more time where storms can feed off the warmer waters, gaining energy to become more intense typhoons before they hit land.

Scientists believe that additional typhoons are likely to develop this year with the potential for further impacts to Japan or east China.

articles.title: The singles choosing IRL dating events over apps
articles.text:
Checking in at a dating event in a bar in Guildford, Olivia Miller-Davis is understandably apprehensive.

Even bringing a friend with her doesn't remove the awkwardness at the start of the night.

"It's always nerve-wracking when you're meeting new people," the 28-year-old admits before downloading an app that will match her to other daters based on their star signs.

This is speed dating 2026-style and Olivia, like many people we speak to, is here because she's fed up of "endlessly swiping" or as some describe it "app fatigue".

She says she hates judging people with "really limited information and just a couple of pictures" because she doesn't feel she can "really fully commit" with so little to go on.

According to a recent study from online regulator Ofcom 11% of adults use dating sites but it suggests the time we spend on them is dropping, from a peak of almost four hours a month in 2023, down to three hours last year.

Olivia's first match on the night is Edward and he agrees that recent dating trends leave him feeling cold.

"I'm fed up with apps," he says.

"I mean, they're designed so that you don't find 'the one', because they want you to come back and use the app forever. They don't want you to get married from the app."

The event is organised by Love at First Sign, a dating company that uses an app to match people based on astrological connection, but most people are just using it as an icebreaker.

Director of events Lissy Cleminson says the way people date is changing and a big factor is more home working since Covid, which means people do not meet in offices or on the commute.

"The little meet-cutes don't happen so much when you're at home with your shirt up top and your pyjamas down bottom," she jokes.

Those running apps are quick to point out online is still a big part in the way people meet.

New research from Match Group, which owns Tinder and Hinge, suggests that out of those who had ever had a romantic relationship, about 21% of baby boomers surveyed met their most recent partner at a pub, bar or club.

Among Gen Z, it was just 4%.

The survey of 3,007 single people also suggests that of those who had ever had a relationship, 20% met their most recent partner on a dating app and 20% met through friends.

Chine Mmegwa, head of strategy, corporate development and operations at Match Group, said Tinder has made tweaks to its service in the past year to win back younger daters.

As well as helping users find out more about each other in advance of dates, through interactive music and astrology features, it has introduced "double date mode" for friends who want to date together.

And she said Tinder is doing more to encourage people to connect IRL. "They want to be in person. You've seen us launch events across the US and now the UK. We are bringing IRL experiences into the app.

"What we're doing is putting IRL into our experience. And so we are bringing that gap to what they're looking for in person, using the apps."

In Guildford, Olivia says her night was a success because she met some men she might want to go on a first date with.

When pushed by the BBC on whether she thought she had met "the one", she laughs and becomes understandably guarded.

"No, I'm not going to name anyone specific. But you'll be invited to the wedding if there is one!"

articles.title: I have a condition people are too embarrassed to talk about
articles.text:
This report contains detailed descriptions of medical symptoms.

Monica Thomas was in her teens when she started experiencing intimate itching and soreness, but despite numerous trips to the doctors it was dismissed as thrush.

Her symptoms got worse, with sores and blisters leaving her in constant pain.

"I was bed bound for quite a long time because I couldn't walk," she says.

Monica says she was examined 28 times in six months before being offered a biopsy.

She says "we don't really talk about" gynaecological health as a society so there is a taboo around speaking about symptoms.

"Even when we go to the doctors, for me, the embarrassment of having to get undressed...with these doctors looking it is embarrassing," she says.

"But equally when you're in pain or it's itching and you've got discomfort, living with it is just as bad."

The 34-year-old from Suffolk was eventually diagnosed with a condition called lichen sclerosus.

The lifelong inflammatory condition affects genitals and can cause white patches to form with itching, soreness, splitting and tears, says Dr Nighat Arif, a GP specialising in women's health.

It affects men and women but is more common in women over 50, external. There is also a small risk of vulval cancer., external

"It's very sore to have sexual intercourse, to pass urine and it gets mixed up with sexually transmitted diseases but it's not contagious," she tells BBC Radio 5 Live podcast That Time of the Month.

Research into the prevalence of vulval lichen sclerosus is limited but analysis by the University of Bristol of people in the West Midlands and Warwickshire estimated it affects about 1% of women.

Dr Sophie Rees, who helped conduct the research, tells the BBC: "This is almost certainly an underestimate, as we know that there is often a very long delay to diagnosis, and some people probably go their entire lives undiagnosed.

"There is unfortunately a lot of shame and embarrassment around seeking help for vulval symptoms, as well as a lack of awareness, even amongst healthcare professionals."

She adds: "More research is badly needed into true prevalence."

Monica says multiple misdiagnoses had a "significant" impact on her mental health.

"I didn't know how to go on... with having no answer, it was just a horrific, lonely time."

She was given medication for herpes. "I was very upset in an appointment with a dermatologist who got quite angry with me because I was like, 'it's not that'.

"Then she said that she wanted me to have blood tests for HIV."

Doctors told her she was "too young" to have lichen sclerosus.

"But sadly, women do have it at all ages, you can have it as a child. So I found that really quite difficult, but I always knew that it wasn't right."

Monica believes there should be more support for those with lichen sclerosus.

"Once you have a diagnosis, you're still necessarily not treated in the manner that you should, I don't even get a checkup," she says.

"I manage it on my own with my steroid cream and hope that I'm doing everything right."

According to the NHS website,, external the cause of lichen sclerosus is unknown. It might be caused by the immune system mistakenly attacking and damaging your skin.

It is not contagious, caused by an infection or by poor personal hygiene. Rubbing or damage to the skin can trigger the condition or make it worse.

"I'd never heard of lichen sclerosus and also I had a cancer that I'd ever heard of in a place I'd never heard of.

"That was the first time I heard the word vulva, no health professional had mentioned it, so it was a lot to take in at that time."

Clare had been in remission from vulval cancer for seven years, when a regular check-up revealed a cancer recurrence and she underwent surgery three years ago.

In June another check up found pre-cancerous cells and she had a sixth surgery.

Clare believes if she had been diagnosed with lichen sclerosus earlier, her cancer may have been diagnosed before it got to stage three.

"I had to have radiotherapy twice and that's left me with instant early menopause, lymphoedema and nerve damage."

Monica encourages women experiencing any changes to their body to keep a diary.

"It's really important that we get to know our bodies better, to know what's normal for you in your private parts as well, because actually our vulvas do change.

"If you are being dismissed, get multiple opinions, just keep going back because you don't have to live without answers."

She recommended the Lichen Sclerosus Guide, external which has a diagram and template to help you talk to doctors.

articles.title: Shakahola cult leader Paul Mackenzie guilty of 191 murder charges in Kenya
articles.text:
The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, has been found guilty of murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.

Mackenzie ordered members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".

His doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil".

Twenty-eight other leaders of his cult were also convicted of murder. They had all pleaded not guilty, repeatedly insisting that nobody was forced to die.

Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.

Delivering her eight-hour judgement in the port city of Mombasa, Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece".

One of his co-accused said Mackenzie had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows".

Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings". Those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus", the judge said.

One witness stated that a pregnant woman had been barred from nursing her new-born baby, who died 12 days later. "She was instructed to fast to death and follow her children," the witness said.

Mackenzie's former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, was initially accused but then entered a plea deal and became a witness for the prosecution.

Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult also face a raft of other legal cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children.

But this is the first time the pastor has faced a verdict on the most serious charges of murder. He is due to be sentenced on 6 November.

He was arrested in 2023, after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast, where Mackenzie had led his followers from across the country.

Stephen Mwiti, 48, said he lost all six of his children to the cult. His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie.

"I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court.

"All six of my children died in Shakahola forest," Mwiti said ahead of the verdict, visibly emotional holding a photograph of his family. "I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel."

Seventeen men were hired from the nearby town for the horrifying task of digging up the shallow graves. Some were paid just $8 (£6) a day.

"Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old."

"We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another."

Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".

Although many of Mackenzie's followers were from elsewhere in Kenya, some of the remains are of people who were familiar to the community because the people in the cult would often go to nearby Shakahola town for supplies and to fetch water from the River Galana which flows through the town.

"We would sometimes carry people on our motorbikes into the forest," said Salim Karisa, another gravedigger. "But it was so planned and secretive that nobody could tell what was happening inside."

Many of the bodies are still unidentified owing to their advanced state of decomposition.

In the court documents, several are referred to as "unknown male child" and identified by the location of their grave and date of their discovery.

Despite the suffering endured by Mackenzie's followers, men, women and children who died due to starvation, strangulation and even being bludgeoned to death, as well as his own suffering, Shukrani believes Mackenzie was "a good person who cares for me".

"Mackenzie didn't force anyone to fast. People made those choices by themselves because of their beliefs," Shukrani said before the verdict was announced.

"I still love him and he is still my pastor."

In contrast Dan Mackenzie believed his father should be found guilty of murder.

"He was the leader, he was someone who they were looking [up to]. So he is a murderer of mass killing," also speaking before the verdict.

articles.title: Robert Kabera: Critic of Rwandan President Paul Kagame found beheaded in Uganda
articles.text:
A former Rwandan army sergeant major, who became an outspoken critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded in neighbouring Uganda.

Robert Kabera, 50, fled Rwanda after being accused of sexual assault, which he denied. He sought asylum in neighbouring Uganda, citing political persecution.

Ugandan police spokesperson Kituuma Rusoke on Monday said that Kabera's head had still not been recovered. His body was discovered by local residents on the outskirts of Kampala over the weekend.

The Rwandan government has not publicly commented on the killing. Several critics of Kagame have been killed, both in Rwanda and abroad.

His widow, Jeanne d'Arc Rwigema Uwizeye, told BBC Great Lakes in a written message that she now feared for her family's safety.

"It is scary. I feel crazy, the children and I don't have security," she said.

According to his family, Kabera had travelled to inspect a construction site about 45 km (30 miles) outside Kampala before his death.

Kabera built a public profile as a musician and YouTuber, attracting more than 144,000 subscribers to his channel, which featured over 800 videos, many criticising Kagame and his administration.

Reacting to news of his murder, exiled opposition group Rwanda National Congress (RNC) called for a thorough investigation and for those responsible to be brought to justice.

In a statement on X, the RNC said: "Today, his family is grieving, his voice is gone, and Rwandans in exile are confronting a terrifying question: where can we be safe?"

His death adds to concerns about the safety of Rwandan dissidents living in exile.

In 2014, Patrick Karegeya, a former Rwandan intelligence chief who helped set up the RNC, was found dead in his hotel room in Johannesburg, South Africa.

Karegeya fell out with President Paul Kagame and was arrested twice, serving an 18-month prison sentence for insubordination and desertion before fleeing to South Africa in 2007, where he became a vocal critic of the government.

Following his death, Kagame made remarks widely seen as a warning to other critics.

"Any person alive who may be plotting against Rwanda, whoever they are, will pay the price. Whoever it is, it is a matter of time," he said.

In 2019, South African authorities issued arrest warrants for two Rwandans accused of murdering Karegeya.

articles.title: Vinted blocks French looters listing stolen goods for sale
articles.text:
Vinted says it has removed listings of items believed to have been looted from shops during the ongoing riots in France.

The second hand re-selling platform said following the weekend's disorder it had "taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to looting".

Shops across several French cities were broken into and ransacked during the outbreak of riots over the weekend.

"The sale of stolen goods, or soliciting them, is strictly prohibited on Vinted, and we have zero tolerance for it," a spokesperson for the company said.

Widespread looting was reported across Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas after protests against the cost of living and public spending turned into riots, leading to the arrests of at least 1,200 people.

More than 2,000 businesses were directly impacted by the weekend's violence, according to the head of the Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI).

Alain Di Crescenzo told France's broadcaster RTL that the riots led to hundreds of millions of euros worth of damage.

Groups of rioters, some wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings as well as looting businesses.

Those that stole goods now appear to be looking to sell them on fast.

"Since this weekend, our teams have taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to the looting, and we have stepped up monitoring of suspicious listings," Vinted told the BBC.

"When our rules are breached, we act against the accounts involved, up to permanent bans."

The company said it was working with French authorities and the police, and was adapting its "processes to detect and counter emerging risks and malicious behaviour".

eBay has not noted any increase in listings linked to the looting in France, but said it works with law enforcement to investigate suspected stolen goods and takes appropriate action, including removing listings and taking action against sellers, when authorities confirm an item is stolen.

articles.title: Home sellers cut asking prices on 3,000 properties a day, says Rightmove
articles.text:
Home sellers cut asking prices on more than 3,000 properties a day on average in Britain during September, according to figures from Rightmove shared exclusively with the BBC.

The property website said the total was the highest of any month for 15 years and was driven, in part, by a glut of homes on the market and some sellers setting unrealistic expectations.

The proportion of listed homes that eventually had a price cut peaked in 2023 and has remained relatively high since.

One seller - Stewart, from Leicester - said some properties were being filtered out of buyers' search results.

He sold one property, and was now selling his late mother's, and both included an element of leasehold which more buyers have been avoiding. However, he said no one thing defined whether a property would sell at a certain price.

"Part of the issue is trying to work out the right selling price. Properties were on the market high and low but were not selling," he said.

He turned down an offer made on his home a day after it was listed. It was below the asking price and he held out for better offers that never came. In the end, he sold after 18 months for £30,000 less than the original asking price.

Colleen Babcock, of Rightmove, said: "Once a home has been on the market for a while and then has a price reduction, some buyers start asking questions, even when there is nothing wrong with the property.

"In a market with so much choice, first impressions matter."

Property portals say buyers are now having to be choosy, with many working to a tight budget as mortgage rates have risen to three-year highs.

articles.title: Musk and Anthropic pledge share giveaways
articles.text:
Elon Musk's SpaceX and artificial intelligence giant Anthropic have pledged big financial giveaways as Big Tech firms come under pressure over the potential impact of AI on humanity.

Musk said on Monday that he would give one of his shares at his rocket company, which owns xAI, to every child in America next year.

The billionaire's announcement came after Anthropic said it would commit 5% of its shares to a fund that will make donations for the "public good".

Anthropic is laying the ground for a potential blockbuster stock market listing that could value the firm at more than $1tn (£750bn). SpaceX set the record for biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history in June, raising $85.7bn.

The pledges come at a time when the AI industry is under intense scrutiny over safety concerns and fears about its impact on society and jobs.

Details over how each American child would be handed a share in SpaceX have not been disclosed.

In a post on social media,, external Musk said: "Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many."

It came after he responded to Anthropic's public fund pledge with: "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public. This is what I will be doing."

Anthropic said none of the shares held in its Public Benefit Fund would be used for lobbying or political donations in the US or overseas.

The Claude developer said on Sunday that the fund could also receive another 2% of the firm's shares at its board's discretion.

Last week, Anthropic told prospective investors that its revenue surged by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.6bn) in the three months to the end of September.

In common with other AI firms, it is seeking to position itself as being able to generate huge profits despite spending billions on developing the technology and building infrastructure to power its models.

Companies around the world, primarily technology firms, have cut thousands of jobs after investing in AI, with many pointing to higher efficiencies from its adoption.

Research by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) published in 2024 suggested that almost 40% of jobs around the world will be affected by AI, with that figure rising as high as ​60% in advanced economies.

In September, a researcher who quit Anthropic said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.

"I believe that if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," he said.

Jacob Coxon was speaking to the BBC after his resignation post on the dangers of AI went viral on a backdrop of growing safety concerns about the industry.

The 27-year-old's former boss, Anthropic head Dario Amodei, had previously called for AI development to slow down - though some have questioned the motivations behind this.

The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Musk, have both said they agree with Amodei's proposal for industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development.

Earlier this month, US President Donald Trump and the heads of major AI firms signed a "morally binding" document, making them responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.

Trump has repeatedly rejected the idea of laws to control development of the technology despite a debate about the potential risks of AI and what it means for humanity.

articles.title: Bereaved families could face 'unjust' tax bill after civil service pension delays
articles.text:
Bereaved families affected by severe delays paying out civil service pensions could face an "unjust" tax bill, the government has been warned.

Under HMRC rules, certain lump sum pension payments must be paid within two years of the pension scheme being notified of a death to remain tax-free.

Conservative MP Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs Parliament's Public Accounts Committee, said it was "unconscionable" some families could face a "death tax" through no fault of their own.

The Cabinet Office said that if delays caused a tax charge there were existing avenues to claim compensation, such as the Pensions Ombudsman.

However, the ombudsman is currently advising that standard complaints are only likely to be resolved within 18 months, with more complex cases facing a longer wait.

The Civil Service Pension scheme manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK.

Outsourcing firm Capita took over the administration of the scheme from a company called MyCSP in December 2025, saying it inherited a backlog of more than 86,000 cases.

Despite a two-year transition period to prepare for the takeover, problems have persisted and by February the backlog had grown to 120,000 cases.

Retired civil servants and bereaved families have been left waiting months for pension payments, with some struggling to pay bills.

According to the latest figures up to 30 September, external, 1,643 outstanding cases of bereavement or death in service are more than 100 days old.

Of these, only 301 are in scope to be paid within 15 days.

The PCS union, which represents civil servants, said that while not all these cases would ultimately be affected by the two-year tax rule, there were "serious questions" over how long they would remain unresolved.

If someone dies before the age of 75, a pension lump sum death benefit is only tax-free if it is paid within two years of the pension scheme first becoming aware of the death, and if the value is below the deceased's Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance.

The payment would be taxed at the same rate as the beneficiary's income tax rate.

Sir Geoffrey has written to Cabinet Office Minister Louise Haigh to urge the government to confirm the bereaved families affected will not face this "unjust financial penalty".

His letter came after BBC Radio 4's Money Box Live highlighted the potential tax liability.

Sir Geoffrey said "the chaos currently engulfing the Civil Service Pension Scheme means that the likelihood of death benefit payments being made within two years is slim".

He warned "a significant number" of family members "will be watching the clock quickly tick down to a year, as the maladministration of the scheme enters its tenth month".

He added: "This is an additional stress they should not have to bear."

Rob Wassell, 58, has been waiting almost two years for the lump sum from his brother's civil service pension, following his death.

On 22 October it will be two years since the pension scheme was notified of his death so if he does not receive the payment in just a few days times, it could face being taxed.

Rob, who contacted the BBC's Money Box programme about his case, said he had been phoning Capita with increasing "desperation" as his situation dragged on.

"It's a bitter pill to swallow to have to pay tax for something which was not my fault," he said.

"It creates unnecessary worry and anguish through the process, which is already in itself difficult."

Rob said he needed the money to cover the estate costs he had to pay for his brother and fill a £20,000 hole in his savings.

However, he said it was "heartbreaking" to hear of other cases where people needed the money just to survive.

Rob added that the idea that he might face "another battle" to recoup the tax through compensation made it feel like "you just want to give up".

Fran Heathcote, head of the PCS union, said it would be "a profound injustice" if families faced a further financial penalty because of Capita's failures.

"If that does happen, the government should be ashamed that families are being made to pay the price for failures that are entirely outside their control," she said.

A spokesperson for the Cabinet Office, which has overall responsibility for the Civil Service Pension Scheme, said: "The service levels following the move to Capita have been completely unacceptable and we are committed to ensuring no member is left financially worse off.

"We are continuing to hold Capita to account, including holding back nearly £10m in payments, and are doing everything in our power to ensure that individuals do not experience delays.

"If delays cause a tax charge, existing avenues for complaints can provide financial redress or compensation to cover losses."

A Capita spokesperson said: "We are deeply sorry for the frustration that the administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme has caused members and their families.

"Our teams are working tirelessly to resolve outstanding cases as quickly as possible, with particular focus on people who have been waiting the longest and those facing financial hardship or challenging personal circumstances."

articles.title: People playing loud music on buses could face £100 fine
articles.text:
Passengers who play loud music on buses in England could be fined up to £100 under an attempt by the government to crack down on antisocial behaviour.

The measures also seek to tackle littering, vaping and threatening behaviour to help improve journeys on all forms of public transport.

Offenders on buses could be issued with the fines under new powers for local authorities.

There have been laws against playing loud music, as well as singing, on trains since 2005 but the government will remind rail passengers of this with the launch of a national campaign asking people to "share the carriage, not the noise".

The proposed crackdown has been welcomed by campaigners, but some have questioned how it can be enforced.

"We've all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone. It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey," said Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

The phenomenon has been given many terms - including loudcasting or sodcasting - and in recent years, Ofcom, YouGov and Transport for London (TfL) have all published polls showing the vast majority of people dislike it.

The rail campaign will be launched across operator websites, social media, and in carriages.

Under existing powers, those who are asked to stop and refuse could be removed from a train or fined up to £1,000.

The government also said it had issued new guidance to local authorities on powers - which were introduced earlier this year - to help them crack down on loud music and other antisocial behaviour on buses in England.

These new powers allow them to impose new rules on buses, but still need to be signed off by the transport secretary.

Those who commit offences could face fixed penalties of up to £100.

The government says bus drivers will not be responsible for enforcing the new rules. It says authorised officers, including Transport Safety Officers and the Police, will deal with the incidents.

Commenting on how fines will be enforced, Chris McDonald, Minister for Science, Research and Innovation, told BBC Breakfast that passengers can complain to staff "or the British Transport Police if they wish".

"They don't have to tackle the individual themselves if they don't feel confident to do that," he said.

Justin from Newcastle-upon-Tyne, welcomed the proposal but wanted to know how it would be enforced.

He told the BBC noise on public transport had stopped him from using buses "due to the levels of antisocial behaviour including this unwanted attendance to someone's social media doom scrolling audio concert".

He said he'd "much rather enjoy my own company with my own music in the isolation of my car".

Transport for London, which operates London Underground, already has by-laws in place to prohibit people playing music or content aloud.

It said that in the first instance enforcement officers will ask the passenger to stop.

"Most people comply at this stage," it said, but added that if someone refuses, they may be asked to leave the train or they could be reported for possible prosecution.
